title: Beginner Pack 2
subtitle: Questions, Shared Topics & Requests
label: 3 patterns · 6 questions
rationale: Builds directly on Pack 1’s A は B です, A の B, and A に B が あります: (1) adding sentence-final か turns Pack 1 statements into polite yes/no questions, (2) replacing は with も marks a second topic sharing the same description, and (3) pairing Level 1’s 下さい with counters (一つ, 二つ, 三つ) lets learners politely request the items introduced in Pack 1.
description: Ask polite yes/no questions with か, connect shared topics with も (“also / too”), and make everyday requests with を下さい.

patterns.pattern: A は B ですか
patterns.readingNote: Add か at the end of a polite です sentence with rising intonation to ask a yes/no question.
patterns.summary: Adding か after です turns a statement (“A is B”) into a polite question (“Is A B?”) without changing word order.

examples.japanese: ここは駅の入り口ですか。
examples.reading: ここは えきの いりぐち ですか。
examples.gloss: ここ here · 駅 station · 入り口 entrance · か question particle
examples.english: Is here the entrance to the station?

examples.reading: あの ひとは おとな ですか。
examples.gloss: あの人 that person · 大人 adult · か question particle

questions.japanese: ここは駅の入り口ですか。
questions.reading: ここは えきの いりぐち ですか。
questions.gloss: ここ here · 駅 station · 入り口 entrance

choices.text: Is here the entrance to the station?
choices.explanation: That’s right! ここは駅の入り口です means “Here is the entrance to the station,” and sentence-final か turns it into the polite question “Is here the entrance to the station?”

choices.text: Here is the entrance to the station.
choices.explanation: Not quite. That translation ignores the sentence-final particle か, which turns the statement into a yes/no question.

choices.text: Are there two entrances at the station?
choices.explanation: Not quite. ここは駅の入り口ですか asks whether “here (ここ)” is the station’s entrance (です + か), not how many entrances exist (二つありますか).

followUp.prompt: Follow-up check — What does this new sentence mean?
followUp.reading: あの ひとは おとな ですか。
followUp.gloss: あの人 that person · 大人 adult

choices.explanation: Not quite. あの人は大人です is a statement, whereas the final か in 大人ですか makes it a question (“Is that person an adult?”).

choices.text: Is that person a big mountain?
choices.explanation: Not quite. 大人 (おとな) means “adult,” not 大きい山 (“big mountain”).
That’s right! あの人は大人です states “That person is an adult,” and か at the end asks “Is that person an adult?”

workedExample.reading: あの ひとは おとな ですか。
workedExample.breakdown: Step 1: Start with the statement あの人は大人です (“That person is an adult”). Step 2: Add か at the end (大人ですか) to ask a yes/no question: “Is that person an adult?”

questions.prompt: Choose the particle at the end that turns this statement into “Is that mountain Mt. Fuji?”:
questions.reading: あの やまは ふじさん です（　）。
questions.gloss: あの山 that mountain · ふじ山 Mt. Fuji

choices.explanation: Not quite. In polite sentences, の links two nouns (A の B); after です, a polite yes/no question takes か (ですか).
That’s right! Placing か right after です (ふじ山ですか) turns “That mountain is Mt. Fuji” into the polite question “Is that mountain Mt. Fuji?”
Not quite. を marks the direct object before a verb and cannot follow です at the end of a sentence.

followUp.prompt: Follow-up check — Choose the particle that turns this statement into “Is this the hotel’s entrance?”:
followUp.japanese: これはホテルの入り口です（　）。
followUp.reading: これは ホテルの いりぐち です（　）。
followUp.gloss: これ this · ホテル hotel · 入り口 entrance

choices.explanation: That’s right! か after です (入り口ですか) turns the statement into “Is this the hotel’s entrance?”
Not quite. に follows a noun to mark location or destination, not the end of a です question.
Not quite. を marks a direct object before an action verb, not a sentence-final question.

workedExample.japanese: これはホテルの入り口ですか。
workedExample.reading: これは ホテルの いりぐち ですか。
workedExample.breakdown: Step 1: これはホテルの入り口です states “This is the hotel’s entrance.” Step 2: Attach か after です (ですか) to ask a polite yes/no question.

patterns.gloss: A is also B / A too
patterns.readingNote: も replaces the topic particle は directly (never say はも).
patterns.summary: When a new topic (A) shares the same description (B) as something already mentioned, use も (“also / too”) in place of は.

examples.japanese: あの女の人も大人です。
examples.reading: あの おんなの ひとも おとな です。
examples.gloss: あの女の人 that woman · も also / too · 大人 adult
examples.english: That woman is also an adult.

examples.reading: この かわも おおきい です。
examples.gloss: この川 this river · も also / too · 大きい big

questions.prompt: Choose the particle that means “That woman is ALSO an adult”:
questions.targetMeaning: That woman is also an adult.
questions.reading: あの おんなの ひと（　）おとな です。
questions.gloss: あの女の人 that woman · 大人 adult

choices.explanation: Not quite. あの女の人の大人 would try to make 大人 belong to あの女の人 (“that woman’s adult”) rather than saying she is also an adult.
Not quite. を marks the direct object of an action verb and cannot link a topic to 大人です.
That’s right! も replaces は to mean “also / too,” giving あの女の人も大人です (“That woman is also an adult”).

followUp.prompt: Follow-up check — Choose the particle that means “This mountain is big, TOO”:
followUp.reading: この やま（　）おおきい です。
followUp.gloss: この山 this mountain · 大きい big

choices.explanation: Not quite. を marks the direct object of an action verb, whereas 大きいです describes the topic.
That’s right! も replaces は after この山 to express “This mountain is big, too.”
Not quite. に marks a location or destination, not “also / too.”

workedExample.reading: この やまも おおきい です。
workedExample.breakdown: Step 1: この山は大きいです means “This mountain is big.” Step 2: Replace は with も (この山も) to add “also / too”: “This mountain is big, too.”

questions.japanese: ここもビルの入り口です。
questions.reading: ここも ビルの いりぐち です。
questions.gloss: ここ here · も also / too · ビル building · 入り口 entrance

choices.text: Here is the only entrance to the building.
choices.explanation: Not quite. も means “also / too,” which implies there is another entrance as well—the opposite of “only.”

choices.text: Here is also an entrance to the building.
choices.explanation: That’s right! ここも means “here, too / here also,” and ビルの入り口です means “is an entrance to the building.”

choices.text: Is here the entrance to the building?
choices.explanation: Not quite. There is no sentence-final か, so this is a statement with も (“also”), not a question.

followUp.prompt: Follow-up check — What does this new sentence mean?
followUp.reading: この かわも おおきい です。
followUp.gloss: この川 this river · も also / too · 大きい big

choices.explanation: That’s right! この川も marks “this river, too,” and 大きいです states that it is big.
Not quite. There is no か at the end; も after この川 means “this river, too.”

choices.text: There is a big river here.
choices.explanation: Not quite. “There is a river” uses 川があります; この川も大きいです means “This river is big, too.”

workedExample.reading: この かわも おおきい です。
workedExample.breakdown: Step 1: この川 (“this river”) + も (“also / too”) sets the topic as an additional item. Step 2: 大きいです (“is big”) describes it.

patterns.readingNote: When requesting a specific number of items, the counter (一つ, 二つ, 三つ) can sit between を and 下さい.
patterns.summary: Mark the item you want with を and finish with 下さい (ください, “please give me”) to politely ask for something at a shop, table, or counter.

examples.reading: りんごを ふたつ ください。
examples.gloss: りんご apple · 二つ two things · 下さい please give me

examples.reading: これを ひとつ ください。
examples.gloss: これ this · 一つ one thing · 下さい please give me
examples.english: Please give me one of these.

questions.reading: りんごを ふたつ ください。
questions.gloss: りんご apple · 二つ two things · 下さい please give me

choices.text: There are two apples under the table.
choices.explanation: Not quite. Although 下さい uses the kanji 下, 下さい (ください) means “please give me,” not 下 (した, “under”) or あります (“there are”).
Not quite. “To lower something” is 下げる (さげる); 下さい (ください) is the polite request word “please give me.”
That’s right! りんごを marks apples as the requested item, 二つ specifies “two,” and 下さい means “please give me.”

followUp.prompt: Follow-up check — What does this new sentence mean?
followUp.reading: これを みっつ ください。
followUp.gloss: これ this · 三つ three things · 下さい please give me

choices.text: There are three of these here.
choices.explanation: Not quite. “There are three” would end with 三つあります, whereas 下さい asks “please give me.”

choices.text: Please give me three of these.
choices.explanation: That’s right! これを marks “this,” 三つ specifies “three things,” and 下さい politely requests “please give me.”

choices.text: Please give me two of these.
choices.explanation: Not quite. 三つ (みっつ) means “three things,” whereas “two things” is 二つ (ふたつ).

workedExample.reading: これを みっつ ください。
workedExample.english: Please give me three of these.
workedExample.breakdown: Step 1: これを marks the item you want (“this”). Step 2: 三つ states the quantity (“three things”). Step 3: 下さい means “please give me.”

questions.prompt: Choose the word that completes “Please give me one box”:
questions.gloss: 箱 box · 一つ one thing

choices.explanation: That’s right! 箱を一つ下さい uses A を + counter + 下さい to politely say “Please give me one box.”
Not quite. あります means “there is” and takes が (箱が一つあります), not the object particle を.
Not quite. います means “there is” for living beings and takes が, whereas 箱を一つ下さい requests a box.

followUp.prompt: Follow-up check — Choose the particle that marks みず (water) as the item requested in “Please give me water”:
followUp.gloss: みず water · 下さい please give me

choices.explanation: Not quite. の connects two nouns (A の B), whereas 下さい needs the object particle を.
Not quite. に marks a location or destination, not the item requested with 下さい.
That’s right! を marks みず (“water”) as the object of 下さい (“Please give me water”).

workedExample.breakdown: Step 1: Name the item you are asking for: みず (“water”). Step 2: Mark it with を. Step 3: Add 下さい (“please give me”).

sources: Komorebi Level 1 curriculum (data/level-1.json): kanji 山, 入, 口, 人, 大, 女, 川, 下, 一, 二, 三 and vocabulary ふじ山, 山, 入り口, 大人, 人, 女, 川, 大きい, 下さい, 一つ, 二つ, 三つ.
JLPT N5 grammar progression (local Renshuu reference IDs): sentence-final question か (37#3 / 741#1), inclusive topic particle も (117#2), and polite noun request A を下さい (333#1).
